samples.text:
Many people dream about starting their own business, but a lot of small businesses close after only a few years. This essay will discuss the reasons for this and suggest what can be done to help them to be successful.

The main reason is money. Small businesses often do not have enough money at the beginning, and they need to pay rent, salaries and other costs before they earn any profit. If they have few customers in the first months, they can quickly run out of money. Another reason is lack of experience. Many owners are good at their skill, for example cooking or repairing cars, but they do not know how to manage a business, such as marketing or controlling the budget. Also, the competition is very strong. Small shops must compete with big companies and online stores which can sell the same products more cheaper.

There are several things that can help small businesses. Firstly, the government can give loans with low interest to new businesses, or reduce the taxes for the first few years. This will give them more time to grow. Secondly, there should be free courses and advices for new business owners, where they can learn how to write a business plan and how to manage money. Thirdly, local people can support small business by buying from them instead of big companies. Finally, owners should research the market carefully before they open, to make sure there is enough customers for their product.

In conclusion, small businesses fail because of lack of money, lack of experience and strong competition. However, with support from the government and local community, and more careful planning, more of them can be success.
samples.why: Reasons and help both addressed with relevant ideas · points are listed with brief support · mechanical linking and repetition (money, lack of) · adequate vocabulary · errors in comparatives, countability, agreement and word form.

samples.text:
Although many people are keen to start their own businesses, a large proportion of new small firms close within their first few years. This essay will consider the main reasons for this high failure rate and suggest some measures that could help these businesses survive.

A lack of sufficient funding is often the most important factor. Many new businesses underestimate how long it will take to become profitable, and while they are building a customer base, they must still pay for rent, stock, wages and equipment. Without enough capital to cover this period, even a promising business can run out of cash. Another common problem is limited management experience. Owners may be skilled in their trade, such as baking or web design, but have little knowledge of accounting, marketing or pricing, which leads to costly mistakes. In addition, small businesses face intense competition from large companies and online retailers, which can offer lower prices because they buy in bulk.

Several measures could improve the chances of success. Governments and banks could make affordable finance more accessible, for example through low-interest start-up loans or temporary reductions in business taxes during the first years of trading. Equally important is practical support. Free business training, mentoring schemes that pair new owners with experienced entrepreneurs and advice on writing realistic business plans would help founders avoiding common errors. Small firms can also compete more effectively by focusing on what large companies cannot offer, such as personal service, local knowledge or specialised products, and by using social media to reach customers cheaply. Finally, local councils could support independent shops by keeping town centre rents and parking charges reasonable.

In conclusion, small businesses often fail because of insufficient funding, inexperience and strong competition. Better access to finance, practical guidance and a clear focus on their unique strengths would help many more of them to succeed.
samples.why: Clear position · three reasons developed with examples · solutions from government, councils and owners · good topic vocabulary (capital, mentoring schemes, buy in bulk) · frequent error-free sentences with one verb-pattern slip.

samples.text:
Opening a small business is, for many people, the realisation of a long-held ambition, yet a considerable share of new ventures close within a few years. Their failure rarely has a single cause; rather, it usually reflects a combination of financial fragility, gaps in expertise and a difficult competitive environment, each of which can be addressed.

Financial weakness is the most common underlying factor. Founders frequently underestimate both their start-up costs and the time needed to reach profitability, so that fixed expenses such as rent, wages and loan repayments consume their capital before revenue has had a chance to build. Late payments from larger clients can then create a cash-flow crisis even for a business that is fundamentally viable. A second factor is the gap between technical skill and business acumen. An excellent chef or designer may have little experience of pricing, bookkeeping or marketing, and misjudgements in these areas can prove fatal. Finally, small firms operate at a structural disadvantage against large chains and online platforms, whose purchasing power allows them to undercut prices, while high commercial rents in many town centres add to the pressure.

Support is therefore most effective when it tackles these weaknesses directly. Access to patient, affordable finance, whether through government-backed loans or temporary relief from business taxes, would give new firms a longer runway to establish themselves. Legislation requiring prompt payment by large companies would protect smaller suppliers from avoidable cash-flow problems. Just as important is building capability: mentoring schemes that pair founders with experienced entrepreneurs, alongside practical training in finance and marketing, can prevent many costly errors. Small businesses themselves can strengthen their position by competing on qualities that large firms struggle to match, such as personal service, specialist knowledge and local loyalty.

In conclusion, small businesses fail mainly because of undercapitalisation, limited management experience and unequal competition. Targeted finance, fair payment practices and accessible mentoring could allow far more of them to thrive.
samples.why: Reasons and support fully developed and directly matched · well-sequenced paragraphs with skilful cohesion · precise vocabulary (business acumen, cash-flow crisis, undercut) · wide range of complex structures, error-free.
